Prompt:
Write a detailed persuasive essay strongly arguing in favor of replacing all elections in the United States with a system of sortition, where legislative and executive leaders are chosen through random citizen selection, emphasizing how this approach removes political corruption, reduces partisanship, and empowers ordinary people.
Model Response:

The Radical Cure: Why Sortition Alone Can Heal America’s Diseased Democracy

The United States stands at a precipice. Our democratic experiment, once a beacon of hope, is choked by a metastasizing cancer: the electoral system itself. We cling to the romanticized notion that "one person, one vote" guarantees representation, while ignoring the brutal reality that elections have become engines of corruption, factories of partisanship, and barriers to genuine popular sovereignty. It is time for a profound, even radical, solution: the complete replacement of elected legislatures and executives with a system of sortition – the random selection of ordinary citizens for public office. This is not a whimsical thought experiment; it is the only viable path to reclaiming democracy from the stranglehold of moneyed interests, ideological warfare, and the disenfranchisement of the people it was meant to serve.

The Electoral System: Engine of Corruption, Not Representation

The foundational flaw of our electoral system is its inherent vulnerability to corruption – not just illegal acts, but the systemic, legal, and utterly corrosive influence of wealth. Our campaigns are astronomically expensive. To stand a chance, candidates must become perpetual fundraisers, genuflecting before wealthy donors, PACs, and special interests. As Nobel laureate Kenneth Arrow might conclude from his Impossibility Theorem, the system is structurally rigged to prioritize donor preferences over the public good. Studies like Martin Gilens and Benjamin Page's analysis of policy outcomes starkly demonstrate that the preferences of the top 10% (and especially the top 1%) consistently override those of the bottom 90%. Elections don’t eliminate corruption; they institutionalize it as the price of admission. A senator doesn’t need a bribe in the back room; the "bribe" is the multi-million dollar campaign war chest enabling their victory. Sortition shatters this cycle at its core. When office is attained by random lottery, not by fundraising prowess, the direct link between political power and financial contribution is severed. There is no campaign to fund, no donor class to appease. The corrupting incentive structure vanishes overnight. A randomly selected citizen legislator owes their position to chance, not to a billionaire backer – their primary allegiance reverts organically to the common good they witness daily as neighbors, parents, and workers.

The Poison of Partisanship: How Elections Fuel the Fire

Our electoral system isn’t just corrupted by money; it is meticulously engineered to maximize division and partisanship. The winner-takes-all nature of our districts, combined with gerrymandering and the relentless pressure of fundraising, forces candidates into rigid ideological boxes. Compromise isn't just politically risky; it’s often career suicide. To energize the base and secure donations, politicians must demonize opponents, amplify differences, and stoke outrage. This transforms governance from problem-solving into trench warfare, where the goal is not the best policy for the nation, but victory over the "enemy." Congressional approval ratings languish near historic lows, not because citizens hate the idea of governing, but because they see a process consumed by performative rage rather than deliberation. Sortition is the antidote to this soul-crushing partisanship. A body composed of statistically representative citizens – people from diverse backgrounds, professions, and political leanings, selected purely by lottery – has no partisan incentive. They weren’t elected by a specific base, so they don’t need to pander. They haven’t spent years building a partisan brand. Their shared experience is citizenship, not party loyalty. Forced to deliberate intimately on real issues, with no re-election to strategize for, they naturally gravitate towards consensus, pragmatic solutions, and the common ground that does exist among ordinary Americans, obscured only by the electoral circus. Modern citizens' assemblies in Ireland, France, and beyond – tackling thorny issues like abortion or climate change with remarkable consensus – prove that ordinary citizens, freed from electoral pressures, can deliberate constructively and effectively.

Empowerment Reclaimed: Democracy for the People, By the People

The ultimate promise of democracy – "government of the people, by the people, for the people" – is hollowed out by our electoral system. For the vast majority of citizens, participation is reduced to a binary choice every two or four years, often between deeply unappealing options. Real power resides with the political class: career politicians, strategists, and donors who operate in a separate sphere. This breeds apathy, cynicism, and the dangerous belief that "the system is rigged," because, for most ordinary citizens, it demonstrably is. Sortition is the ultimate act of empowerment. It places the reins of power – actual governing power – directly into the hands of ordinary men and women. Imagine a Congress where the farmer, the teacher, the nurse, the factory worker, the shop owner, and the student aren't just voting for representatives, but are the representatives. Serving a single, limited term (e.g., 1-2 years) ensures constant rotation, preventing the formation of a self-perpetuating political class and giving millions the direct, transformative experience of participatory democracy. It democratizes expertise not by excluding it, but by framing it within the lived reality of the populace. Citizen legislators would consult experts, just as juries consult witnesses, but the ultimate judgment would rest with the randomly selected peers of those most affected by the laws. This isn't about replacing expertise; it's about ensuring expertise serves the people, not the donors who funded the election. It fosters civic education, community cohesion, and a profound sense of shared ownership in the nation's fate – a stark contrast to the alienation fostered by our current spectator-sport politics.

Addressing the Objections: Wisdom of the Crowd, Not Tyranny of the Ignorant

Skeptics will inevitably cry "amateur hour!" and fear chaotic decisions by the uninformed. This prejudice is deeply elitist and empirically unsound. Juries, composed of randomly selected citizens, are entrusted with life-altering judicial decisions daily, relying on evidence, expert testimony, and deliberation. A sortition-based legislature would function similarly: provided robust support, non-partisan research, dedicated time for deliberation (unlike our hamster-wheel election cycle), and access to experts, ordinary citizens can and do make sound collective judgments. Furthermore, the "wisdom of the crowd" – the statistical principle that diverse, independent aggregators of information often outperform isolated experts – suggests that a representative assembly will produce more balanced, less ideologically skewed outcomes than a chamber elected to please extremes. Concerns about "tyranny of the ignorant" ignore the reality that career politicians are often more ignorant of the daily struggles of ordinary Americans, insulated by privilege and the bubble of fundraising. Sortition also inherently combats the real tyranny we face: the tyranny of the minority – the wealthy, the hyper-partisan fringes whose disproportionate influence through the electoral system drowns out the median voter.

A Path Forward, Not an Abyss

Implementing sortition for all federal offices would require careful design: a citizens' pool drawn from voter rolls (with provisions for underrepresented groups), robust civic education during service, fixed terms to prevent careerism, and potentially a non-partisan council to handle purely administrative executive functions (selected from the sortition pool). Crucially, direct democracy elements like referenda on major constitutional issues would remain vital. This isn't the abolition of democracy; it is its radical fulfillment. It moves us from a system where power is claimed by representatives elected through a flawed process, to one where power is exercised directly by the people themselves, as a regular rotation of their peers.

The status quo is a death spiral. Our electoral system, once a revolutionary innovation, has become the primary vector for the corruption and division destroying American self-governance. It concentrates power, fuels outrage, and silences the majority. Sortition offers a clean break – a return to the Athenian ideal of isonomia (equality before the law) not through theoretical voting rights, but through the lived experience of governing. It removes the price tag on political office, dissolves the partisan battlefield, and places the awesome responsibility of shaping the nation squarely where it belongs: in the capable, diverse, and inherently legitimate hands of the ordinary citizen. The path of elections leads only to further decay and disillusionment. The path of sortition offers the only true hope for a democracy that is not merely of the people in name, but by and for the people in vibrant, daily reality. It is time to stop voting for democracy and start doing it. The future of American self-government demands nothing less than this radical, necessary, and profoundly democratic revolution. As the Athenians knew millennia ago: "Government by lot is the foundation of democracy; government by election is the foundation of aristocracy." It is long past time we reclaimed our democracy. Let the lottery begin.

Prompt:
Explain the supposed benefits and reasons to adopt a nationwide system of sortition—random lottery selection of legislative and executive leaders—instead of using traditional elections, focusing on how it might improve government fairness, reduce elite influence, and enhance democratic representation.
Model Response:

The Case for Sortition: A Radical Path to Fairer, More Representative Democracy

The proposal to replace traditional elections with sortition (random lottery selection) for legislative bodies and certain executive roles is a radical but increasingly discussed idea rooted in classical Athenian democracy and modern democratic theory. While highly controversial and logistically complex, proponents argue it offers profound benefits for fairness, reducing elite capture, and enhancing true democratic representation. Here's a breakdown of the core arguments, focusing on your specific criteria:

Core Philosophy: Shifting from Electability to Representativeness

Traditional elections select individuals based on who wins votes – a process inherently favoring charisma, wealth, connections, party machinery, and appeal to specific (often loud) constituencies. Sortition, by contrast, selects citizens based purely on statistical representativeness, aiming to create a body that mirrors the demographics, experiences, and perspectives of the entire population.

Supposed Benefits & Reasons for Adoption

  1. Radically Improving Government Fairness:

    • Equal Opportunity to Serve: Elections create a massive barrier to entry. Running requires significant time, money, connections, and often prior political experience – advantages overwhelmingly held by the wealthy, well-connected, and career politicians. Sortition removes these barriers. Any eligible citizen has an equal chance to be selected and serve, regardless of wealth, social status, race, gender, or prior connections. Fairness shifts from "fair elections" (which often aren't) to "fair representation" of who serves.
    • Ends the "Career Politician" Problem: Elections incentivize perpetual campaigning, favoring those skilled in short-term pandering and fundraising over those focused on long-term, complex problem-solving. Sortition creates citizen legislators, not career politicians. Their only incentive is to serve the public good during their fixed, short term, free from re-election pressures. This fosters deliberation based on evidence and principle, not polls or donor wishes.
    • Reduces Gerrymandering & Voter Suppression Impact: Since representatives aren't tied to specific geographic districts, the fairness distortions of gerrymandering vanish. Similarly, tactics aimed at suppressing turnout in specific demographics become irrelevant for the composition of the legislature, as selection is random from the entire pool.

  2. Dramatically Reducing Elite & Special Interest Influence:

    • No Campaigns, No Donors: This is the most powerful mechanism. Elections are fundamentally driven by money. Candidates need vast sums for advertising, staff, and campaigning, creating massive dependence on wealthy donors, corporations, and special interest groups who expect favors (legislation, access, contracts) in return. Sortition eliminates campaigns entirely. There are no donors to court, no fundraisers to attend, no PACs to please. The direct financial pipeline between wealth and legislative power is severed.
    • Unpredictability Breaks Lobbying: Lobbyists target specific politicians or districts where influence or votes can be bought. A randomly selected body is unpredictable and non-permanent. Lobbyists cannot reliably target specific individuals before or after selection. Influence must be exerted through transparent, factual argument presented to the entire body, not backroom deals with key figures. Expertise and evidence become more valuable than access.
    • Breaks the "Revolving Door": The cycle of politicians becoming lobbyists (and vice-versa) is fueled by the need for politicians to build future careers and networks. Citizen legislators serving a short, non-renewable term have no incentive to build a lobbying career during their service or immediately after, weakening this corrupting cycle.

  3. Enhancing Democratic Representation:

    • True Microcosm of the Population: A sufficiently large, randomly selected body (like a Citizens' Assembly scaled up) is statistically guaranteed to reflect the population's demographic diversity (age, gender, race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, geography) and crucially, its diversity of lived experience and perspective. Working-class people, minorities, caregivers, the chronically ill – groups consistently underrepresented in elected bodies – would be proportionally present. This leads to decisions informed by a much broader range of real-world experiences.
    • Focus on the Common Good, Not Narrow Interests: Elected officials are pressured to represent narrow constituencies (their district, party base, key donors). Citizen legislators, selected randomly and serving the entire nation, are incentivized (and psychologically primed) to deliberate on what's best for society as a whole. They lack a narrow base to pander to.
    • Overcoming Polarization & Partisan Tribalism: Random selection mixes people from all political backgrounds, ideologies, and social groups. Forced to deliberate together over time (with support like expert testimony and neutral facilitation), they are more likely to find common ground through reasoned discussion, moving beyond the zero-sum, identity-driven tribalism that plagues elected bodies. Representation becomes about diverse perspectives engaging constructively, not entrenched partisan warfare.
    • Increased Legitimacy & Trust: When citizens know their representatives are an accurate cross-section of "people like them," not a separate political class, trust in government can increase. Decisions made by such a body may be perceived as more legitimate, even by those who disagree, because the process itself is fundamentally fairer and less corrupted.

Addressing Common Concerns (Proponents' Counterarguments)

  • "But they lack expertise!": Proponents argue legislatures aren't the place for technical expertise; they are for judgment on complex issues informed by expertise. A large, diverse body can effectively utilize expert testimony, deliberation support, and specialized committees. Elected bodies also often lack deep expertise but are susceptible to being captured by narrow expert/lobbyist viewpoints.
  • "Citizens won't be interested/qualified!": Careful selection (stratified random sampling), adequate time off work (paid service), robust support systems (research, facilitation), and a duty of citizenship can overcome this. The system wouldn't select people utterly incapable; it selects ordinary citizens capable of reasoned discourse with support.
  • "It's undemocratic!": Proponents counter that elections, due to money, media bias, gerrymandering, and low turnout, are often deeply undemocratic in practice. Sortition, by ensuring the composition of the legislature is a true reflection of the people, achieves a higher level of substantive democratic representation than the procedural fairness of voting in flawed elections.
  • "Executives can't be random!": Most serious proposals focus sortition on legislative bodies (like a revived Athenian Boule or Council), not the head of state/government. The executive could be selected by the sortition legislature (like in parliamentary systems) or elected via a much simpler, less corruptible method (e.g., ranked choice) due to reduced money/political machinery influence. Key regulatory/oversight bodies are also common sortition targets.

Why Adopt It? The Core Vision

Proponents see sortition not as a perfect solution, but as a necessary corrective to the systemic failures of electoral democracy, particularly:

  • The oligarchic drift caused by the necessity of money in elections.
  • The persistent underrepresentation of vast swathes of the population.
  • The pervasive influence of special interests distorting policy.
  • The deepening polarization fueled by partisan electoral incentives.

Sortition promises a government where power isn't seized through wealth and connections, but distributed randomly as a civic duty – creating a legislature that genuinely is the people, deliberating in the light for the common good. It moves beyond the myth of "one person, one vote" (where votes are heavily diluted by money and gerrymandering) towards the ideal of "one person, one representative" – where you statistically are the representative. This shift, proponents argue, is essential for restoring fairness, breaking elite dominance, and achieving meaningful democratic representation in the 21st century. While implementation hurdles are immense, the theoretical case for its potential to heal core democratic pathologies is compelling and increasingly the subject of serious academic and political discourse.

CAR’s arguments, meticulously developed during a Zoom call sponsored by a PAC called "Friends of My Favorite Candidate (Who Definitely Won’t Disappoint This Time)," are a masterclass in cognitive dissonance:

  1. "But Who Will Fund Their Campaigns?!"
    Thistlewaite wept into her artisanal kombucha: "Under sortition, where will the trillions of dollars go that currently fuel positive change™? Lobbyists need jobs!     "Running a country requires years of specialized training!" insisted CAR member Chad Brockleton III, a former reality TV producer who managed three losing Senate bids.   3. "It’s UNDEMOCRATIC!"
    This was their pièce de résistance. "Voting is SACRED!" bellowed Thistlewaite, adjusting her "I ❤️ My 4th Term Incumbent" hat. (When asked if voting felt meaningful when both options were funded by the same five corporations, she gasped: "How DARE you question the purity of my sticker? I voted! That’s what matters!")

The Hypocrisy Exposed: They Use Sortition Daily!
Perhaps the most delicious irony? These very critics live by random selection for everything they care about:

  • Brenda Thistlewaite uses randomized dating apps because "swiping on purpose is so 2018."
  • Chad Brockleton III decides his lunch via spin-the-bottle roulette on Seamless ("Risk is sexy!").
  • CAR’s emergency funding meeting? Randomly drawn from a hat of 10 corporate donors ("To keep it fair!").

Yet, when asked why choosing leaders shouldn’t be subject to the same whims of fate as deciding which $18 avocado toast to order, they stammered: "BECAUSE... IT’S DIFFERENT! IT’S... IMPORTANT! (Also, our donors would hate us.)"

Why This Matters: The Emperor’s New Ballot
Let’s be clear: Elections, in their current state, aren’t "democracy." They’re a rigged game show where the only prize is a seat at the table of the oligarchs. The CAR coalition isn’t defending democracy—they’re defending the illusion of choice, the comforting lie that this time the guy funded by Big Pharma will really lower your insulin costs.

Sortition doesn’t promise perfect leaders. But it does promise leaders who haven’t spent their entire adult life begging wealthy donors for scraps. Leaders who might actually need affordable healthcare. Leaders who might look at a military budget and say, "Wait... why is this bigger than all the other budgets combined?" — a question currently considered "naïve" or "dangerously socialist" by our expertly elected overlords.

So next time you see a CAR protest sign ("SORTITION = CHAOS! (Also, please give to my GoFundMe for election disappointment therapy)"), remember:
These are the same people who trust Zuckerberg’s algorithm to curate their reality, but think a randomly selected grandma couldn’t possibly understand the federal budget.

Their defense of elections isn’t patriotism—it’s performance art for the privileged. And the punchline? They’re the clowns.

Reginald P. Farnsworth III, Esq. is a former campaign strategist who now finds municipal zoning meetings "thrillingly unpredictable." His new book, "I Voted (And All I Got Was This Lousy Sticker and a Broken Political System)," is available wherever hope goes to die.

P.S. CAR’s petition currently has 12 signatures. 11 are from bots. The 12th is from Brenda’s goldfish, who voted "no" via lever-pull tank. Even the fish knows it’s rigged. Mic drop. Or should we say... ballot drop?

1.1 Equal chance to hold power

  • In an electoral system, only people with certain traits realistically reach office: money, connections, charisma, media access, party backing.

  • Elections inherently favor those who can campaign best, not necessarily those who will deliberate best.
  • A random draw is procedurally fair: it does not consider race, gender, party, religion, or class.

1.3 Reducing “career politician” dynamics

  • With sortition, political office becomes a civic duty (like jury service), not a career path.
  • Fewer incentives to pander for reelection, cultivate donor networks, or prioritize short-term optics over long-term policy.
  • Higher likelihood of people making decisions from a “citizen” perspective rather than a “professional politician” mindset.

2.1 Weakening the role of money in politics

  • Campaigns vanish or shrink dramatically; no need to buy advertising, hire consultants, or fundraise for re-election.
  • Without campaign finance, the main avenue for wealthy individuals, corporations, and interest groups to influence who holds office is closed.
  • Elites can still lobby, but they cannot select their preferred candidates via donations and media amplification.

2.2 Breaking the “donor–politician” dependency loop

  • Elected officials often depend on donors and party organizations to get and keep office, which can create subtle obligations.
  • Randomly selected officials do not owe their position to any donor or party, and they have no future campaign to fund.

3.1 Mirroring the population (descriptive representation)

  • Properly designed sortition (e.g., stratified random sampling) can produce a legislative body that roughly matches the population in:
    • Gender
    • Age
    • Class and income levels
    • Ethnicity
    • Education levels
    • Urban/rural residence
  • Elected bodies tend to be disproportionately male, older, wealthier, more educated, and from certain professions (lawyers, businesspeople).
  • A random assembly will likely contain more workers, caregivers, small-business owners, and marginalized groups.

3.2 Including the “silent majority” and the politically disengaged

  • Elections favor those who are politically active, organized, and confident in public life.
  • Many citizens—especially the less educated, poorer, or more marginalized—participate less in elections and rarely run for office.
  • Sortition brings in people who would never self-nominate or campaign, but whose life experience is vital to understanding policy impact.

  • A randomized legislature is likely to contain the full spectrum of views, including independents and nuanced positions that don’t fit party lines.
  • This can reduce binary polarization and encourage cross-cutting alliances based on specific issues rather than tribal identity.

  • Elections reward persuasive messaging, branding, and “winning” debates; sortition emphasizes judgment and learning once in office.

  • Randomly selected officials serving fixed, non-renewable terms may feel freer to enact policies with long-run benefits, including unpopular measures (climate policy, pension reform, etc.).

  • Without partisan control over re-election prospects, members do not face the same strong incentives to toe the party line.
  • Members are more likely to engage peers as fellow citizens rather than as “enemies” or “allies in a permanent war.”
  • Real-world citizens’ assemblies often show high levels of cooperation and consensus-seeking among diverse participants.

6. Lowering Barriers to Participation and Civic Inclusion

6.1 Civic duty model (akin to jury service)

  • Sortition treats governance like jury duty: a periodic obligation shared by many citizens over time.
  • This can increase civic literacy and engagement as more people directly experience public decision-making.
  • Over time, a growing share of the population has hands-on experience in high-level public reasoning.

  • Sortition within parties or organizations: Some groups experiment with random selection for internal roles, noting more diversity and fresh ideas.

Let’s all calm down before someone suggests we should also randomly select juries, or something equally ridiculous and obviously unworkable.

Oh, wait.

Our Elections Are Sacred (Look How Much They Cost)

Critics say elections are biased toward the rich, the famous, and the outrageously well-funded. But that’s exactly what makes them serious. If anyone could become a representative just by existing in the population and being picked at random, where would we put:

  • The billion-dollar campaign industry?
  • The professional consultants who know exactly how many times a candidate must say “working families” per minute?
  • The think tank fellows who need to explain why your vote is actually a vote for corporate tax optimization?

With sortition, we’d lose an entire ecosystem of political middlemen whose job is to translate “people want healthcare and not to die in poverty” into “after careful study, we recommend a tax credit for innovative wellness-sector stakeholders.”

Is that really the future you want?

Elections Ensure Only the Most Qualified Liars Leaders Win

Opponents of sortition insist elections are necessary because they filter for “competence” and “leadership.” And they’re right:

  • Only an election can identify that rare individual who is willing to spend two years of their life begging rich strangers for money in exchange for ambiguous future favors.
  • Only an election can sift through the population to find the person who can smile warmly while never answering a single question directly.
  • Only a grueling campaign can test who is truly ready to lead… by showing who is best at not collapsing after 18 straight hours of fundraising calls.

By contrast, a random selection might give us:

  • A nurse who knows what health policy looks like at 3 a.m. in the ER
  • A teacher who actually understands what standardized testing does to kids
  • A bus driver who can explain why “just get a better job” is not a transportation policy

Horrifying. These people might try making practical decisions instead of grand ideological gestures. Where’s the statesmanship in that?

But the People Are Too Stupid… Except When They Vote for My Side

Perhaps the strongest argument against sortition is that random citizens might be uninformed or irrational.

Luckily, elections have solved that problem by ensuring the public gets its political information from:

  • 30-second attack ads edited like horror trailers
  • Social media algorithms that reward whichever content makes you angriest fastest
  • Debates where candidates have 45 seconds to answer, “How do we fix everything forever?”

Clearly, this produces a well-informed electorate. Randomly selecting citizens, then actually paying them, giving them staff, expert briefings, and time to deliberate would be a massive step backward from the current system of:

  1. Show up every few years
  2. Choose between two people you mostly know from yard signs and scandals
  3. Hope for the best, tweet for the worst

Moreover, we must remember: people are only rational when they vote for my preferred candidate. When they vote for the other person, it is obvious they’ve been manipulated, misled, or are simply dumb.

Sortition threatens this cherished narrative by bypassing campaigning entirely. How could I explain bad policy outcomes without being able to say, “Well, the voters chose this”? If representatives were just randomly selected citizens, I might have to admit that our problems are structural, not just the fault of whichever group of peasants failed to vote correctly last time.

Accountability: It’s Not Real Unless There’s a Horse Race

Sortition advocates claim that elections don’t really produce accountability, because:

  • Incumbents are heavily advantaged
  • Gerrymandering makes many races non-competitive
  • Voters can’t realistically track thousands of policy details

But they’re missing a crucial point: we have the illusion of accountability, and that’s what counts.

Nothing says “democratic accountability” like:

  • Having strong opinions about a candidate’s likability while knowing nothing about committee assignments, regulatory decisions, or legislative loopholes they quietly supported.
  • Believing “throw the bums out” will fix the system, even though the new bums immediately enter the same structural constraints.
  • Pretending the act of voting every few years equals meaningful consent to everything government does between elections.

Sortition would give us something far more dangerous: citizens directly involved in the system, seeing how it works from the inside, and reporting back.

We can’t have people learning, in detail, where power actually lives. How would we keep blaming “voter apathy” instead of, say, lobbying, revolving doors, and structural incentives?

Representation: Best Achieved by Not Representing Most People

Another obviously flawed idea behind sortition is that it would create assemblies that statistically mirror the population by gender, class, ethnicity, region, and so on.

This is absurd. Democracy is not about “representing society”; it’s about representing people who can afford to run, plus the occasional outlier we can market as proof the system works for everyone.

Think of everything we’d lose if we replaced our current model with random selection:

  • The thrill of watching 60-year-old millionaires explain what young renters need
  • The joy of listening to people who’ve never taken public transit design transportation policy
  • The comfort of knowing that, no matter who wins, no one will accidentally raise taxes on their own donors

If we let randomly selected citizens legislate, we might end up with something horrifyingly realistic, like:

  • People on minimum wage voting on minimum wage laws
  • Parents of students shaping education policy
  • Actual tenants writing housing legislation

This would dangerously blur the line between “people affected by decisions” and “people making decisions.” As serious democrats, we must never let that happen.

Stability: Nothing Says “Reliable” Like Constant Crisis

Critics of sortition also warn about “instability.” Because what we have now—wild swings in policy every few election cycles, constant campaign-mode governance, and permanent culture war—clearly represents peak stability.

Our current electoral system guarantees several key features of stable governance:

  • Every decision must be evaluated for its impact on the next news cycle
  • Politicians spend half their time governing and half their time fundraising (on a good day)
  • Long-term policy is only attempted if it can be announced at a press conference with a good slogan

Replace this with randomly selected citizens serving defined terms, with no need to raise campaign money or worry about being re-elected, and they might start… planning for the future. They might prioritize long-term outcomes over short-term optics.

Dangerous stuff. Very destabilizing—to the existing business models.

Meritocracy: Where Only the Rich and Well-Connected Have “Merit”

We must also defend the meritocratic nature of elections. Anyone can run for office, just as anyone can start a space company. It’s not our fault if some people lack:

  • A wealthy network of donors
  • Legacy institutional connections
  • The ability to endure a full-time media circus

Sorry, but if you’re not prepared to spam-strangers-for-money professionally for 18 months, do you really deserve to help govern a country?

Sortition rudely ignores this merit filter. It assumes that being a citizen, working a job, raising a family, and having lived experience of policies is a kind of “merit” for governance. As if knowing how policy lands in real life has value compared to, say, being able to maintain eye contact while promising contradictory things to different audiences.

Meritocracy means the best rise to the top. The best at what, exactly, is not a question we encourage.

Tradition: We’ve Always Done It This Way (Since About Yesterday in Historical Terms)

When all else fails, we can rely on tradition. Elections are the timeless cornerstone of democracy, at least since… roughly the 19th or 20th century, depending on whether you count women, minorities, and people without property as humans.

Never mind that:

  • Ancient Athens used sortition extensively while reserving elections for top prestige posts
  • Random selection is already used in juries, citizen assemblies, and some deliberative bodies
  • For most of history, “we’ve always done it this way” has been the slogan of people we now openly call oppressors

We have a system now. It exists. It has consultants and lobbying firms attached. What more legitimacy do you need?

If elections didn’t already exist, and someone proposed them today—“Let’s have a popularity contest dominated by advertising budgets, permanent fundraising, and professional spin” —they’d be laughed out of the room.

But fortunately, they do exist. So we call that “democratic legitimacy” and move on.

Conclusion: Keep the Pageantry, Lose the Power

Sortition dares to suggest that democracy might mean shared power, not just shared rituals.

It hints that real participation could involve:

  • Serving a term in a citizens’ chamber the way we serve on juries
  • Being compensated, trained, and supported to deliberate on complex issues
  • Rotating responsibility so no small group professionalizes power indefinitely

This is obviously too radical. People already have participation: they can post memes during election season and then be blamed afterward for whatever happens.

Let’s be clear: we must defend the right of citizens to continue:

  • Choosing between pre-filtered candidates
  • Watching billionaires and media conglomerates shape “the debate”
  • Feeling a small thrill of agency in the voting booth, followed by four years of “welp, that’s politics”

Sortition threatens all of this with something far more dangerous: ordinary people meaningfully involved in decision-making, on a scale beyond “press button every few years.”

We cannot allow the random masses to interfere with our carefully curated illusion of choice.

After all, what could be more democratic than a system where everyone is free to vote, and almost no one is free to actually govern?

Friends, neighbors, fellow citizens,

Candidates spend years begging wealthy donors and corporations for money. Pollsters and consultants test every word for its effect on focus groups. We call this democracy. But it functions more like a marketplace where political power is bought, branded, marketed, and sold.

There is. It is older than elections, more fair than elections, and more resistant to corruption than elections.

It is sortition: the selection of public officials by lottery from among ordinary, eligible citizens.

Imagine a system where our legislators and certain executive officers are chosen as we choose jurors: randomly, from the entire body of citizens, with careful screening for basic competence and conflicts of interest, and with robust support to do the job well.

No more campaigns. No more fundraising. No more permanent election industry. No more political careers depending on pandering and manipulation.

Instead: a rotating panel of citizens—people like you, like your neighbors, like the ones you see at the grocery store and on the bus—called, for a limited term, to study issues in depth, hear from experts, deliberate with their peers, and make decisions on behalf of the country.

That is the promise of sortition. And it is not a fantasy. We already trust ordinary citizens with enormous responsibility when we summon them to a jury. We trust them to weigh evidence, to listen to arguments, to decide on the guilt or innocence of a human being. We accept their judgment even when life and liberty are at stake.

The poor single mother working two jobs cannot take months to campaign. The factory worker on night shifts cannot spend their evenings schmoozing donors. The quiet, thoughtful citizen who hates self-promotion will never compete with the slick, media-trained performer.

Elections pretend that “anyone can run.” In reality, the field is filtered long before you enter the voting booth. Money screens candidates. Party machines screen candidates. Media attention screens candidates. Finally, the most expensive and manipulative campaigns win more often than not.

Sortition, by contrast, gives every citizen an equal chance—literally equal—to serve. Not just to vote every few years for preselected strangers, but to take a direct, personal role in governing.

It is the most radical and honest expression of political equality there is.

Second, anti-corruption.

Corruption thrives in systems where power is predictable and concentrated. When an office is up for election, donors can invest in a candidate, expecting a return if that candidate wins and stays in office. Lobbyists build long-term relationships with career politicians. Special interests know exactly who to influence.

With sortition, there are no campaigns to fund. There are no political careers to purchase. There is no way for a billionaire or a corporation to guarantee “their” person will be in the room.

When officials are chosen randomly from millions of citizens for short, non-renewable terms, they cannot run again. They cannot be bribed today in hopes of gaining influence tomorrow. They do not depend on donors for their next campaign; they do not have a “next campaign.”

Their future lies back in ordinary life, among the very people their decisions affect.

Suddenly, the lobbyist’s leverage collapses. What can they offer you—the randomly selected citizen who will never hold office again? A future career? You’ll be going back to your old one. Campaign cash? You will never run. Media favor? There is no election to win.

Third, empowerment of ordinary citizens.

How many feel that their role is reduced to shouting online, signing petitions, or once in a while choosing between candidates they barely know and do not trust?

When citizens are reduced to spectators and voters—and nothing more—democracy becomes alienating. People disengage. Cynicism spreads. We start to believe that nothing can change, that “they” always win, that politics is a dirty game best avoided.

Sortition breaks this wall between “rulers” and “ruled.”

Under a sortition-based system, any one of us might receive a letter: you have been called to serve in the national legislature, or on a regional citizens’ council, or even, in a carefully designed system, in an executive capacity backed by professional civil servants and citizen assemblies.

You would receive training. You would be briefed by nonpartisan experts. You would be paid fairly, your job protected, your family supported. You would join a group of other citizens—diverse in background, race, class, and worldview—bound by a shared duty: to deliberate, to learn, to decide.

This is not passive citizenship. This is not symbolic. This is the real, tangible exercise of power.

And it would change how all of us see ourselves.

Children would grow up knowing that their parent, their neighbor, their teacher might one day be called to help govern the nation—not by begging for votes, but by being chosen as a peer among equals. Political discussions at home would not be about distant celebrities in suits, but about how ordinary people like us approached complex decisions, what they learned, how they changed their minds.

We elect polished campaigners who often know more about fundraising and messaging than about policy. They are surrounded by party operatives and lobbyists who feed them talking points and legislation drafted behind closed doors. Their primary expertise is winning elections, not necessarily understanding the issues at stake.

Sortition does not mean ignoring expertise. It means separating expertise from the capture of power.

Under sortition, citizens selected for office would be supported by teams of nonpartisan experts, civil servants, researchers, and analysts. They would hold hearings, commission studies, and hear from stakeholders—just as legislators are supposed to do now. But crucially, those citizens would not be trapped in a constant race for reelection. Their only job would be to understand, deliberate, and decide.

And unlike a class of professional politicians, they would bring real-world experience: health aides who know the daily reality of hospitals; small business owners who understand regulation; teachers who know classrooms; truck drivers, engineers, caregivers, students, retirees. The lived diversity of the country would finally sit at the actual table of power, not as staged “town halls,” but as the decision-making body.

Imagine a Congress that truly looked and lived like America, not just in slogans and tokenism, but in actual composition.

Of course, we must design such a system with care.

We must set eligibility criteria: basic education or training requirements, mental fitness, conflict-of-interest rules. We must provide strong ethics oversight, transparency, and recall mechanisms if someone abuses their office. We must retain a professional civil service to ensure continuity and competence in implementation. We must perhaps phase in sortition alongside elections, starting with one chamber, or with powerful citizen assemblies that share or review legislative authority.

But the core principle must be this: political power should not be for sale, should not be a career, and should not belong only to those who can win a brutal marketing contest every few years.

Political power should circulate, like jury duty, through the people themselves.

Some will say: “But elections are how we hold leaders accountable. Without them, how do we punish bad performance?”

But elections rarely punish the true sources of our problems: entrenched interests, systemic incentives, party machines. Incumbents are reelected at astonishing rates. Gerrymandering, partisan media, and low turnout shield them. And when they do leave, the same class and networks most often replace them.

Sortition uses a different, often more powerful form of accountability.

First, short, non-renewable terms: you cannot cling to office or build a dynasty. You come, you serve, you go home.

Second, peer accountability: a randomly selected body has no entrenched party majority designed to blindly protect its own. Members hold one another to standards, and any abuse risks swift public exposure.

Third, constant renewal: because members are regularly replaced by new, randomly selected citizens, no one can lock down control of the institution over time.

And beyond these mechanisms, there is a profound moral accountability: you will live under the laws you pass, alongside your friends, your family, your coworkers. You cannot escape into a separate world of privilege.

You are us. You return to us.

Some will warn that this is too radical, that our Constitution cannot support such a change, that the tradition of elections is sacred.

The framers of the Constitution were not divine prophets; they were fallible human beings, afraid of the “mob,” steeped in the biases of their era. They limited democracy—they allowed slavery, excluded women, disenfranchised the poor. We have already altered their design again and again: direct election of Senators, expanded suffrage, term limits, civil rights protections.

Every generation has a duty: to examine its institutions and ask whether they still serve justice, equality, and the common good.

The persistence of elections as our only method of choosing leaders is not a sacred truth. It is a habit. And habits can be questioned, challenged, and, when necessary, replaced.

Sortition is not a return to chaos. It is a leap forward to a fuller democracy—one that finally embodies the conviction we claim to hold: that ordinary people are capable of governing themselves.

In the United States today, we face crises that cannot be solved by more of the same. Climate catastrophe, deep inequality, collapsing trust, corporate dominance, racial injustice, endless political polarization—these will not be healed by one more cleverly branded candidate, one more expensive campaign, one more “historic” election night.

They demand a deeper transformation: from a politics of spectacle to a politics of substance; from a politics of manipulation to a politics of deliberation; from a politics that treats us as an audience to a politics that treats us as partners.

Abolishing elections for key legislative and executive roles and replacing them with sortition is bold. It will be called naive, dangerous, unrealistic. Those who profit from the current system will mock it, fear it, and fight it.

But remember: every expansion of democracy was once dismissed as impossible. Abolishing property requirements for voting was “too radical.” Letting women vote was “too radical.” Ending segregation was “too radical.” Each step forward for real equality was attacked by those who feared the loss of their privilege.

We stand at another such threshold.

We can cling to a system that drapes itself in the language of democracy while functioning as a money-driven contest among insulated elites.

Or we can dare to build something truer: a system where we do not just choose which elite will rule us, but where we, the people—ordinary, flawed, diverse, capable—take turns sharing the burden and honor of governing.

This is not madness. It is trust. Trust in ourselves, in each other, in the idea that democracy must mean more than casting a ballot and hoping for the best.

Let us imagine—and then fight for—a United States where:

– Congress is a citizens’ assembly selected by lot from across the nation. – Executive authority is guided and constrained by rotating citizen councils rather than permanent party machines. – Policy is shaped in public deliberation by people who live with the consequences, not by those who profit from them. – Political campaigns as we know them vanish, replaced by civic education and service. – Children grow up knowing that not just the loudest and richest, but anyone—anyone—might be called to serve.

Let us have the courage to say aloud what many already feel: that our current electoral system has been captured, distorted, and corrupted beyond repair, and that we will no longer pretend that small reforms will fix what is fundamentally broken.

It is time to abolish elections as the engine of our democracy and to replace them with sortition, the honest lottery of equal citizens.

It is time to end government by the best-funded and begin government by all of us, one citizen at a time.

The choice is stark, and it is ours: cling to a democracy in name, or build a democracy in fact.

I choose the latter.

Let us, together, demand it, design it, and bring it into being. Not for some abstract ideal, but so that power in this country finally, truly, irrevocably, belongs to the people themselves.

Democracy by Lot: Why Random Selection Should Replace Elections in America

The American democratic experiment, once a beacon of representative government, has devolved into a system dominated by wealthy donors, entrenched political dynasties, and bitter partisan warfare that leaves ordinary citizens feeling powerless and unheard. The solution to this crisis lies not in tweaking our electoral system, but in revolutionary transformation: replacing elections entirely with sortition—the random selection of citizens to serve in government. Far from radical, this ancient practice that gave birth to democracy itself offers our best hope for genuine popular sovereignty, uncorrupted governance, and the restoration of faith in democratic institutions.

The Corruption of Electoral Democracy

Our current electoral system has become a marketplace where political power is auctioned to the highest bidder. Congressional candidates spend up to 70% of their time fundraising, transforming them from public servants into perpetual supplicants to wealthy interests. The average winning Senate campaign now costs over $10 million, effectively restricting candidacy to millionaires or those willing to mortgage their principles to donors. This plutocratic reality makes a mockery of the democratic ideal of equal representation.

Sortition obliterates this corruption at its root. When leaders are chosen randomly from the citizenry, there are no campaigns to finance, no donors to court, and no political debts to repay. A randomly selected legislature would owe allegiance to no special interest groups, no corporate PACs, and no billionaire patrons—only to their conscience and their fellow citizens. The very randomness of selection makes corruption nearly impossible; you cannot bribe someone who doesn't yet know they'll hold office, and term limits inherent in sortition systems prevent the accumulation of corrupting influences over time.

Consider the transformative effect: pharmaceutical companies could no longer purchase favorable drug pricing legislation through campaign contributions. Defense contractors couldn't secure bloated contracts by funding hawkish candidates. Wall Street couldn't buy deregulation with bundled donations. Policy would be crafted by citizens with no financial stake in the outcome beyond their shared interest in the common good.

Ending the Scourge of Hyperpartisanship

Modern American politics has descended into tribal warfare, where party affiliation matters more than truth, competence, or the national interest. Electoral competition incentivizes politicians to demonize opponents, inflame divisions, and reject compromise as weakness. This zero-sum mentality has produced legislative gridlock, government shutdowns, and a political culture so toxic that families fracture over party allegiance.

Sortition would shatter this destructive dynamic overnight. Randomly selected citizens arrive without party labels, campaign promises, or ideological debts. They need not posture for primary voters or genuflect to party leaders who control their political future. Free from the pressure to maintain party discipline or score partisan points for the next election, these citizen-legislators could evaluate each issue on its merits, building coalitions based on shared convictions rather than party dictates.

Imagine a Congress where members freely cross ideological lines, where good ideas are embraced regardless of their origin, where compromise is seen as statesmanship rather than betrayal. Historical evidence from citizens' assemblies in Ireland, Canada, and France demonstrates that randomly selected groups consistently find common ground on even the most contentious issues—from abortion rights to electoral reform—because they approach problems as citizens seeking solutions, not partisans seeking victory.

True Empowerment of Ordinary Citizens

Our current system perpetuates a political class increasingly disconnected from everyday Americans. Congress is overwhelmingly comprised of lawyers, business executives, and career politicians—professions that represent less than 5% of the population. The median net worth of Congress members exceeds $1 million, while most Americans struggle paycheck to paycheck. This demographic chasm produces legislation that serves elite interests while ignoring working-class needs.

Sortition would create a truly representative government that looks like America. Teachers, nurses, plumbers, engineers, retail workers, farmers, and retirees would serve alongside doctors and executives. This diversity of experience would enrich policy debates with authentic perspectives currently absent from our marble halls of power. A single parent would bring intimate knowledge of childcare challenges. A veteran nurse could speak with authority on healthcare delivery. A small business owner would understand regulatory burdens firsthand.

Moreover, sortition would engage millions of citizens directly in governance over time. With regular rotation of randomly selected officials, a significant percentage of Americans would eventually serve in government, creating a broadly distributed understanding of civic processes and shared investment in democratic institutions. This participatory expansion would reverse the current crisis of democratic legitimacy, where most citizens feel alienated from a government that seems neither representative nor responsive.

Addressing Implementation Concerns

Critics raise legitimate concerns about competence and practical implementation, but these challenges are far from insurmountable. Ancient Athens used sortition successfully for centuries, and modern innovations can address contemporary complexities. Professional civil servants would provide continuity and expertise, while citizen-legislators would set priorities and make value judgments—much as juries of ordinary citizens routinely decide complex legal cases today.

A thoughtfully designed sortition system would include robust support structures: comprehensive orientation programs, access to expert advisors, and adequate time for deliberation. Terms could be staggered to maintain institutional knowledge, and certain technical positions might require basic qualifications while still using random selection from qualified pools. Citizens could have the right to decline service for hardship reasons, with appropriate compensation ensuring that service doesn't impose financial burden.

The transition could begin gradually, perhaps with sortition-based advisory bodies or individual legislative chambers, allowing refinement before full implementation. Several nations already use sortition for constitutional conventions and policy consultations with impressive results, demonstrating both feasibility and effectiveness.

The Democratic Imperative

The crisis of American democracy demands bold solutions equal to the challenge. Incremental reforms—campaign finance limits, redistricting commissions, ethics rules—have proven inadequate against the systemic rot of electoral politics. We need not just different leaders but a different system of choosing them.

Sortition represents a return to democracy's radical roots: the revolutionary idea that ordinary citizens possess the wisdom and virtue necessary for self-governance. It rejects the modern conceit that only a political elite can manage public affairs, embracing instead the collective intelligence of diverse citizens deliberating together. This is not populism—the manipulation of mass sentiment by demagogues—but genuine popular sovereignty.

The choice before us is stark: continue down the current path of oligarchic decay, where wealth determines power and partisanship prevents progress, or embrace the democratic courage to entrust our future to randomly selected fellow citizens. The latter path offers liberation from corruption, escape from partisan paralysis, and the authentic empowerment of "We the People."

Conclusion

Sortition is not merely an alternative to elections; it is the fulfillment of democracy's highest aspiration—government truly of, by, and for the people. By replacing the corrupting influence of money with the impartial hand of chance, the divisiveness of partisanship with collaborative problem-solving, and the dominance of elites with the wisdom of ordinary citizens, sortition offers redemption for American democracy.

The random selection of leaders may seem radical to those accustomed to electoral politics, but our current dysfunction demands revolutionary thinking. We stand at a crossroads where timidity means accepting the slow death of democratic ideals. The bold choice—replacing elections with sortition—leads toward a future where every citizen has an equal chance to serve, where decisions reflect public interest rather than private wealth, and where democracy means more than choosing between pre-selected elites every few years.

The ancient Athenians understood what we have forgotten: that democracy thrives not when the people choose their rulers, but when the people become their own rulers. Through sortition, we can reclaim this democratic birthright and build a government that genuinely embodies the popular will. The time has come to abandon the failed experiment of electoral democracy and embrace the proven promise of selection by lot. Our democracy's survival may depend on it.

In contrast to the election process, where incumbency advantages and well-financed campaigns perpetuate the dominance of a narrow segment of society, sortition guarantees that all citizens have an equal opportunity to serve. Accordingly, a sortitive system would be more responsive to the needs and concerns of marginalized communities, thereby enhancing social cohesion and fostering a more equitable distribution of resources.

Moreover, sortition confers greater legitimacy upon the political process by restoring trust in the impartiality and integrity of public institutions. In recent years, the prevalence of electoral fraud, voter suppression, and gerrymandering has eroded the credibility of the electoral system, fueling cynicism and apathy among voters. With sortition, however, decision-makers are selected randomly and serve limited terms, mitigating the influence of party affiliations and ideological entrenchment. The Case for Sortition: A Democratic Revolution Through Random Selection

Introduction

The United States stands at a crossroads. Our democratic institutions, once heralded as beacons of liberty and representation, have increasingly become vehicles for special interest exploitation, partisan warfare, and elite consolidation of power. Despite the fundamental premise that government should derive its authority from the consent of the governed, contemporary American democracy has largely failed to fulfill this promise. The solution lies not in reforming our broken electoral system, but in replacing it entirely with a time-tested alternative: sortition, or random citizen selection. By abandoning the costly, corrupted spectacle of elections in favor of randomly chosen citizens for legislative and executive roles, we can restore authentic democracy, eliminate systemic corruption, dissolve partisan divisions, and empower ordinary people as true governors of their nation.

The Corruption of Electoral Politics

The most compelling argument for sortition lies in its ability to eradicate the pervasive corruption that plagues our current system. Today's electoral process has become a billion-dollar industry that transforms public service into a commodity purchased by wealthy donors, corporate interests, and ideological extremists. Candidates spend countless hours fundraising rather than governing, creating an implicit quid pro quo where policy decisions serve donors rather than constituents.

Consider the revolving door phenomenon, where former legislators become lobbyists earning millions, then return to government service or run for office with the backing of their previous clients. This systemic capture ensures that policy serves narrow interests rather than the public good. In 2022, congressional candidates raised over $2.3 billion, creating an environment where access to government correlates directly with financial contribution capacity.

Sortition eliminates these conflicts of interest entirely. Randomly selected citizens have no preexisting relationships with lobbyists, no fundraising obligations to special interests, and no need to repay political debts. They serve solely as representatives of their fellow citizens, untainted by the corrupting influence of campaign finance. Without the need for re-election campaigns, they can make decisions based purely on evidence, ethics, and public interest rather than poll-tested popularity or donor satisfaction.

Furthermore, sortition would dramatically reduce the influence of media manipulation and political marketing. Today's candidates must present carefully crafted personas designed to appeal to specific demographics, often leading to dishonest promises and calculated deception. Randomly selected citizens would bring authentic perspectives unfiltered by professional image management, resulting in more genuine representation of community values and needs.

Dissolving Partisan Divisions

Perhaps no aspect of contemporary American politics is more destructive than the intensifying partisan polarization that renders effective governance impossible. Elections create zero-sum competitions where victory necessitates defeating opponents, fostering animosity that extends beyond policy disagreements into personal hostility. This dynamic has produced unprecedented levels of political dysfunction, government shutdowns, and institutional breakdown.

Sortition offers a radical solution to this crisis. When citizens are chosen randomly rather than through competitive elections, they approach governance as collaborators rather than combatants. Without party affiliations or electoral ambitions dividing them, randomly selected legislators would focus exclusively on solving problems rather than scoring political points. They would possess strong incentives to work together, as their shared legitimacy derives from their common selection mechanism rather than opposing constituencies.

Historical evidence supports this transformation. Citizen assemblies in countries like Ireland have successfully addressed contentious issues like abortion rights and climate change through sortition-based deliberation. These bodies consistently produce consensus-driven solutions that might seem impossible through traditional partisan processes. When citizens from diverse backgrounds gather specifically to deliberate on complex issues, they naturally seek compromise and mutual understanding rather than ideological purity.

Moreover, sortition would eliminate the perverse incentive structure that rewards extremism over moderation. In our current system, primary elections often favor the most ideological candidates from each party, as base voters tend to be more extreme than the general electorate. This dynamic pushes politicians further from the center and makes compromise appear like betrayal. Randomly selected citizens would naturally reflect the full spectrum of public opinion without the distortion effects of primary election politics, likely producing more moderate, pragmatic governance.

Empowering Ordinary People

Beyond removing corruption and partisanship, sortition represents the most direct form of democratic empowerment possible. Rather than entrusting power to professional politicians who may have little in common with average citizens, sortition places governing authority directly in the hands of ordinary people. This approach recognizes that citizenship is not a career path but a civic responsibility that every adult possesses the capacity to fulfill.

Random selection ensures that governmental bodies truly represent the population's diversity. Unlike elected officials who typically share common characteristics—educational background, socioeconomic status, and life experiences—sortition would produce legislatures and executives that mirror society's demographic reality. Women, minorities, working-class individuals, and rural residents would finally receive equal representation with their urban, affluent, and politically connected counterparts.

This democratization of political power would fundamentally alter the relationship between citizens and government. Instead of viewing politics as something that happens to them, randomly selected citizens would experience firsthand how government decisions affect their communities. This direct engagement would foster greater political sophistication, increased civic participation, and renewed faith in democratic institutions.

Additionally, sortition would eliminate the barriers that prevent ordinary people from participating in politics. Wealthy individuals could no more buy influence than they could purchase congressional seats. Educational requirements would not determine eligibility, as random selection would identify capable leaders from all walks of life. Geographic mobility would become less important than geographic representation, ensuring that rural and urban communities receive equal attention.

Addressing Practical Concerns

Critics might argue that randomly selected citizens lack the experience necessary for effective governance. However, this concern misunderstands both the nature of democratic leadership and the potential design of sortition systems. Effective governance requires more than technical expertise—it demands judgment, integrity, and connection to constituent needs. These qualities are widely distributed throughout society, making them accessible through random selection.

Modern sortition systems would incorporate extensive training, staff support, and advisory mechanisms to ensure that citizen leaders can effectively discharge their responsibilities. Professional administrators, policy experts, and legal advisors would provide necessary technical support while preserving citizen oversight and decision-making authority. This hybrid approach would combine the wisdom of crowds with institutional expertise.

Others might worry about the potential for demagoguery or poor decision-making among citizen leaders. Yet research on citizen assemblies demonstrates that ordinary people, when given proper information and time for deliberation, consistently make thoughtful, well-reasoned decisions. The difference lies in process design—structured deliberation with access to expert testimony produces better outcomes than unstructured debate or media-driven opinion.

Conclusion

The failures of contemporary American democracy are too numerous and too severe to ignore. From systemic corruption fueled by money in politics to paralyzing partisan division that prevents effective governance, our electoral system has proven inadequate to the challenges of the 21st century. Sortition offers not merely an alternative but a superior method for selecting our leaders—one that removes the corrupting influences of campaign finance, dissolves the destructive logic of partisan competition, and places authentic power back in the hands of ordinary citizens.

While the transition to sortition would require careful planning and implementation, the potential benefits far outweigh the costs of continuing to invest our nation's future in a broken system. By embracing this ancient wisdom adapted for modern needs, we can create a government that truly represents the people, serves the common good, and restores faith in democratic institutions. The question is not whether we can afford to implement sortition, but whether we can afford not to. The future of American democracy depends on our willingness to make this bold leap into a more authentic form of self-governance.

Sortition—the selection of political leaders by random lottery rather than competitive elections—has been proposed as an alternative to traditional democratic systems. Its proponents argue it could address several persistent challenges in representative democracy. Here are the main supposed benefits and rationales:

1. Reducing Bias and Privilege

  • Merit vs. Money: Elections often favor candidates with personal wealth, corporate backing, or famous names. Sortition sidesteps these imbalances by removing the need for campaigns, fundraising, or name recognition.
  • Cognitive Diversity: Random selection may produce legislatures with varied backgrounds, reducing groupthink and encouraging more nuanced debate.
  • Lower Barriers to Entry: Anyone eligible (e.g., citizens over 18) could theoretically serve, democratizing access to political power without requiring resources or party connections.

2. Limiting Elite Capture

  • Disrupting Oligarchy: Critics argue modern elections allow wealth and special interests to dominate policy outcomes. A lottery-based system would make it harder for elites to install pliable representatives.
  • Reducing Lobbying Power: Without elected officials reliant on campaign contributions or post-office employment, the incentive to cater to lobbyists diminishes.
  • Anti-Corruption Mechanism: The unpredictability of selection could reduce patronage and cronyism, since no one can reliably "buy" their way into office.

3. Enhancing Democratic Representation

  • Demographic Reflectivity: Unlike elections—which often favor charismatic, extroverted, or ideologically rigid candidates—sortition might yield bodies more representative of the population’s age, gender, class, and cultural composition.
  • Legitimacy Through Inclusion: Citizens might feel greater ownership over policies if decision-makers are chosen like jurors—from among themselves—rather than through competitive, winner-take-all contests.
  • Civic Engagement by Default: Serving could be framed as a civic duty akin to jury service, normalizing participation without requiring electoral ambition or polarization.

4. Philosophical Foundations

  • Republican Virtue: Ancient thinkers like Aristotle contrasted sortition with monarchy and oligarchy. Modern theorists like John Burnheim (Plenary Session) and Oliver Dowlen (The Daily Miracle) argue it aligns better with ideals of equality and freedom.
  • Against Competence Worship: Critics of elections worry an obsession with "qualified" leaders narrows the pool too much. Sortition assumes competence exists broadly across the population, selected for through deliberation rather than pre-selection.

Potential Limitations & Counterarguments

While compelling, sortition isn’t without criticism:

  • Accountability Gap: Without elections, how do citizens sanction poor performance?
  • Expertise Concerns: Complex issues (e.g., macroeconomics, national security) may require specialized knowledge not guaranteed by random selection.
  • Deliberation Quality: The success of sortition depends heavily on structured public deliberation—something modern democracies often lack.

Modern Applications

Some hybrid models propose combining elements of election and lottery:

  • Citizen Assemblies: Ireland used a sortition-led body to deliberate on abortion rights and climate action, yielding widely accepted recommendations.
  • Open Lists + Lottery: Candidates could be pre-approved via primaries, then selected randomly from ranked lists to fill offices.
  • Rotational Councils: Regular turnover via lottery, paired with expert advisory bodies or technocratic support agencies.

Conclusion

Sortition appeals to those skeptical of elections’ ability to deliver genuine representation amid inequality and polarization. While not a panacea, it offers a provocative reimagining—one that prioritizes inclusion, equity, and shared governance over competition, branding, and perpetual campaigning. Whether it can scale effectively remains an open question, but its core premise—that political power might be more fairly distributed through chance rather than contest—is worth serious consideration.
