Empowering Ordinary People

Another key argument for sortition is that it empowers ordinary people by giving them a direct role in governance. The current electoral system often makes citizens feel disconnected from the political process, as if their only role is to vote every few years for candidates who may not truly represent their interests.

  1. True Representation:

    • Sortition ensures that the government is made up of "ordinary" citizens who are more likely to understand and represent the needs and concerns of the average person. This could lead to policies that are more in line with the public interest.

  2. Increased Civic Engagement:

    • Knowing that any eligible citizen could be called upon to serve in a government position might encourage more people to stay informed and engaged in civic matters. This could lead to a more educated and active citizenry.

  3. Democratizing Political Power:

    • By distributing political power more evenly among the population, sortition democratizes the political process. It makes it possible for anyone, regardless of their wealth, social status, or connections, to hold a position of power and influence.

Addressing Potential Concerns

While the idea of sortition has many appealing aspects, it is important to address some potential concerns.

  1. Competence and Expertise:

    • One common criticism of sortition is that randomly selected citizens may lack the necessary expertise to make informed decisions on complex issues. However, this can be mitigated by providing comprehensive training and support for those who are selected. Additionally, a sortition system could still make use of expert advisors and civil servants who provide technical knowledge and continuity.

  2. Willingness to Serve:

    • Another concern is that not everyone who is randomly selected will be willing or able to serve. To address this, a sortition system could include a process for individuals to opt out if they are unable or unwilling to serve, with another random selection made to fill the vacancy.

  3. Accountability:

    • Some might argue that without elections, there is no way to hold officials accountable. However, other mechanisms such as term limits, regular reviews by independent bodies, and the ability for the public to recall officials could be implemented to ensure accountability.

Conclusion

Replacing all elections in the United States with a system of sortition could bring about a profound transformation in the political landscape. For more than two centuries, the United States has treated elections as synonymous with democracy. But elections are not democracy’s essence; they are merely one method—often a deeply flawed one—of selecting leaders. In practice, modern American elections have become a mechanism for concentrating power in the hands of a political class that is dependent on wealthy donors, locked into permanent partisan warfare, and insulated from the lived experience of ordinary citizens. If the goal is a government that serves the public rather than the powerful, then the most direct reform is also the most radical: replace elections with sortition—a system in which legislative and executive leaders are chosen by random selection from the citizenry.

Sortition is not a novelty or a gimmick. It is an old democratic tool used in various forms in ancient Athens and echoed today in juries and citizen assemblies. Its promise is simple and profound: when leaders cannot be bought, cannot be campaigned into office, and cannot be filtered through party machines, the structure of incentives changes. Corruption becomes harder, partisan incentives weaken, and ordinary people gain real governing power. In an era of pervasive distrust and political paralysis, sortition offers not a minor tweak but a structural cure.

Elections have become a market for power—and markets invite corruption

American elections are extraordinarily expensive, and that expense is not incidental—it is the central gateway to power. Candidates must raise massive sums, cultivate donor networks, purchase media attention, hire consultants, and build campaign infrastructures. Even when contributions are legal, the underlying logic is corrosive: politicians learn early that their careers depend not on being good at governing, but on being good at fundraising and messaging.

This creates predictable outcomes:

  1. Donors become the real “primary electorate.” Before the public ever votes, candidates have already been selected by their ability to attract money. Those with access to wealth—personal or networked—start with an enormous advantage.
  2. Lobbyists and special interests purchase sustained influence. They may not literally write a check for a vote, but they fund campaigns, provide future job prospects, supply talking points, and shape legislation through persistent access.
  3. Politicians govern with an eye toward re-election. Even well-intentioned officials face constant pressure to avoid unpopular but necessary decisions, to perform outrage for visibility, and to prioritize short-term optics over long-term outcomes.

Sortition severs this machinery at the root. Randomly selected leaders do not need to fundraise. They do not need to court donors. They do not need to spend half their time dialing for dollars. Most importantly, there is no “campaign marketplace” where money buys attention and attention buys power.

Could corruption still exist under sortition? Of course—any system can be attacked. But the economics shift dramatically. Bribing one randomly selected citizen is not the same as investing in a predictable class of career politicians who depend on financial support year after year. Sortition replaces a stable, targetable political elite with a rotating, hard-to-predict set of citizens who do not need to maintain donor relationships to keep their jobs. That alone makes corruption more difficult, riskier, and less cost-effective.

Elections reward partisanship and punish cooperation

America’s partisan crisis is not merely cultural; it is structural. Elections incentivize division because division mobilizes voters, generates attention, and simplifies messaging. Candidates win by drawing sharp contrasts, energizing base supporters, and framing opponents as threats. Once in office, the same incentives continue: officials know the easiest way to secure re-election is to avoid cross-party collaboration that might alienate their base or weaken their brand.

The result is a politics of permanent campaign:

  • Compromise becomes betrayal.
  • Complex policy becomes slogan.
  • Governing becomes theater.

Sortition changes the job description of leadership. Randomly selected citizens are not running for office. They are not building personal brands. They are not auditioning for cable news or a higher seat. Without electoral incentives, the primary reward becomes solving problems, not winning the next cycle.

Just as jurors can disagree strongly yet still deliberate seriously because they share responsibility, sortition-based leaders would have a built-in reason to cooperate: they must actually complete the work. When you cannot “blame the other side” to win re-election, blame loses its value. When you are there temporarily and will return to normal life, grandstanding loses its payoff. The center of gravity moves from performance to deliberation.

Parties could still exist as voluntary associations and sources of ideas, but they would no longer function as gatekeepers to power. Under elections, parties control nominations, fundraising networks, and media pipelines; under sortition, parties become less like machines and more like think tanks—persuaders rather than selectors. That is a healthier role.

Sortition empowers ordinary people—and forces government to resemble the public

Even at its best, electoral democracy tends to produce a governing class that is older, wealthier, better connected, and more professionally political than the population it represents. This is not because voters explicitly demand it; it is because campaigns select for certain traits: fundraising ability, name recognition, elite networks, and comfort with constant public exposure.

Sortition flips that. Random selection produces a body that actually looks like the country—across income levels, occupations, education backgrounds, regions, and life experiences. Instead of asking citizens to petition a distant class of professionals, sortition makes citizens the governing institution itself.

This has three powerful effects:

  1. Lived experience becomes policy input. A single parent, a nurse, a factory worker, a small business owner, a veteran, a teacher, and a retiree do not merely “have voices”—they have votes in the governing room.
  2. Policy becomes less abstract and more reality-tested. Career politicians often argue about ideology; ordinary citizens are more likely to ask, “Will this actually work? Who pays? Who benefits? What breaks?”
  3. Citizenship becomes meaningful. A democracy is healthiest when people feel they have real agency. Voting once every few years for pre-selected candidates is thin participation. Serving in government—even temporarily—creates widespread civic competence and trust.

Critics sometimes assume ordinary citizens cannot govern. But that assumption is less a fact than a habit of deference. We trust ordinary citizens with jury decisions that can take away someone’s freedom; we trust them to raise children, run businesses, build infrastructure, and staff hospitals. The real question is not whether citizens can govern, but whether a system designed to elevate campaign specialists can ever reliably produce public-serving leadership.

“Random people can’t run a country”—a solvable objection, and not a reason to keep a broken system

The strongest argument against sortition is competence: surely random selection risks placing unqualified people in charge. But this objection confuses selection method with institution design. Sortition does not mean throwing unprepared citizens into chaos. It means designing roles, support systems, and safeguards around citizen leadership.

A workable sortition system would include:

  • Civic training and onboarding comparable to what jurors receive—only more robust, covering constitutional duties, ethics rules, budgeting basics, and policy evaluation.
  • Access to professional expertise from nonpartisan civil servants, auditors, scientists, economists, and legal counsel—structured so experts inform decisions rather than capture them.
  • Deliberative procedures that require evidence, structured debate, and transparent reasoning, rather than rewarding sound bites.
  • Rotation and term limits to prevent the emergence of a permanent political class while ensuring continuity through staggered terms.
  • Ethics enforcement and anti-corruption rules including strict gift bans, mandatory disclosures, and independent investigative bodies.

In many ways, sortition makes competence more likely than elections do, because elections often select for the wrong skills. Campaigning is not governing. Fundraising is not legislating. Viral messaging is not crisis management. Sortition selects citizens, then trains and equips them to do the job—whereas elections select marketers and force them to govern.

Sortition is the most direct way to dismantle political capture

A fundamental problem in American governance is “capture”: institutions that should serve the public become oriented around the interests of those with money, connections, and sustained access. Elections are vulnerable to capture because they create predictable, repeat players—politicians, party strategists, major donors, and lobbyists—who interact constantly.

Sortition disrupts that ecosystem by making the leadership unpredictable and temporary. If you are a special interest trying to influence policy, it is far harder to cultivate long-term relationships with a rotating group of citizen-leaders who return to private life. The cost of capture rises, and the expected benefit falls.

Moreover, because sortition produces a leadership that mirrors the population, it dilutes the disproportionate influence of elite professional networks. Instead of a small club speaking to a small club, you get a room full of people who, by design, cannot all be “from the same world.”

A plausible blueprint: citizen-led legislature, citizen-led executive, professional administration

Replacing elections does not mean abandoning institutions; it means changing who occupies them and under what incentives. A persuasive model could look like this:

  1. A national citizens’ legislature selected by sortition, with members serving limited, staggered terms. Subcommittees handle policy domains and rely on transparent hearings with competing expert testimony.
  2. An executive council selected by sortition, replacing the singular “winner-take-all” presidency with a small group that must deliberate and agree—reducing authoritarian drift and personality cults.
  3. A strengthened, nonpartisan civil service responsible for implementing policy, with clear performance metrics and oversight.
  4. Independent oversight bodies (inspector general functions, anti-corruption agencies, auditors) insulated from the officials they monitor.
  5. A constitutional bill of rights and judicial review unchanged—because sortition should democratize governance without endangering fundamental liberties.

This structure keeps what works—rule of law, professional administration, rights protections—while replacing the elective aristocracy with genuine citizen power.

The moral argument: democracy should mean “rule by the people,” not “marketing to the people”

At bottom, the case for sortition is not only practical but moral. Elections today often reduce citizens to an audience: political professionals perform, donors fund, media amplifies, and voters choose among curated options. The people’s role is reactive.

Sortition restores the people as participants. It treats citizenship as a shared responsibility rather than a consumer preference. It says: you are not merely someone to be persuaded every few years—you are someone capable of governing.

And that shift matters. A nation cannot remain stable when large portions of its population believe government is permanently rigged, permanently purchased, and permanently hostile. Sortition does not guarantee perfect outcomes, but it directly attacks the reasons so many people believe the game is fixed.

Conclusion: sortition is not a utopian fantasy—it is the logical next step

If you want less corruption, you must remove the fundraising-and-influence pipeline that elections intensify. If you want less partisanship, you must remove the winner-take-all incentives that elections reward. If you want ordinary people empowered, you must do more than let them choose between elite-managed options—you must let them govern.

Sortition accomplishes all three at once. It replaces the politics of careerism with the politics of civic duty, the politics of division with the politics of shared responsibility, and the politics of money with the politics of representation by reality. In a moment when faith in institutions is collapsing, the boldest reform is also the most democratic: stop electing rulers and start selecting citizens.

  • Less party gatekeeping: Parties often control who becomes “viable” through endorsements, primaries, and ballot access. A lottery bypasses party filters, which proponents argue reduces oligarchic control by party elites.

  • Closer match to demographics and lived experience: Legislatures are often wealthier, older, more highly educated, and drawn from certain professions (law, business, etc.) compared to the public.   • Representation of ordinary perspectives: Elections can overweight preferences of high-turnout groups and politically active donors/activists. Random selection can pull in citizens who don’t have time or incentives to engage in electoral politics but are still affected by policy.
  • Better coverage of “silent majorities” and dispersed interests: Groups without strong lobbying organizations or concentrated voting blocs can be systematically underrepresented in elections. Sortition doesn’t require organized political power to gain seats.

4) Better deliberation (in theory): decision-making less driven by performance and polarization

Claim: Sortition can shift incentives from messaging to problem-solving.

  • No need for constant “audience signaling”: Elected officials must continually posture for reelection, donors, and party bases. Sortition aims to reduce the payoff to grandstanding and culture-war escalation.
  • More time for structured learning and deliberation: Sortition advocates typically pair random selection with expert briefings, cross-examination, and facilitated deliberation (similar to citizens’ assemblies).   • Reduced polarization incentives: Competitive elections can reward mobilizing the base and demonizing opponents. A randomly selected group may include more moderates and people less invested in partisan identity, potentially lowering the temperature.

5) Anti-corruption logic: fewer transactional relationships

Claim: If officials are not repeat players in an electoral marketplace, quid-pro-quo dynamics become harder to sustain.

  • Short, nonrenewable terms reduce “future favors”: If you can’t run for reelection (or can’t immediately), there’s less reason to trade policy for campaign support.
  • Less revolving-door logic (supposedly): Career officeholders can build networks aimed at post-office lobbying or lucrative appointments. Rotation and strict post-service restrictions are often proposed to blunt that.
  • Randomized oversight and auditing: Many sortition proposals include random selection for oversight boards, ethics panels, or audit committees—making it harder to predict and influence who will scrutinize decisions.

6) Legitimacy as “the people themselves” governing

Claim: Sortition embodies a literal version of popular rule: the government is not merely chosen by the people; it is composed of the people.

  • Democratic equality: Proponents argue that true political equality means not just equal votes, but more equal chances to participate directly in governing.
  • Reduced alienation and cynicism: If citizens see that ordinary people—not just elites—can hold real power, the system may feel less rigged and more trustworthy.
  • Civic education spillovers: Participants return to society with deeper policy understanding, which advocates claim can enrich public discourse and social cohesion.

7) Policy outcomes less biased toward wealthy interests (the hoped-for effect)

Claim: Because randomly selected officials are more economically typical and less donor-dependent, policy should tilt closer to broad public preferences.

  • Median citizen vs. median donor: Elected systems can over-respond to donors and organized interests. A sortition chamber would contain far more lower- and middle-income members, potentially changing priorities (healthcare access, housing, wages, consumer protection).
  • Less “regulatory capture” via relationships: If decision-makers rotate frequently and aren’t career insiders, interest groups have less time to build cozy, durable influence.

8) Why advocates say elections structurally favor elites

Sortition supporters usually aren’t saying elections always fail, but that elections have built-in tendencies:

  • Cost of running is a barrier to entry.
  • Media visibility and branding reward those with resources.
  • Parties narrow choices before the public votes.
  • Strategic voting and districting can distort representation.
  • Political careers create a semi-permanent governing class.

From this view, lottery selection is attractive because it directly attacks those structural advantages rather than trying to regulate around them (campaign finance laws, anti-gerrymandering reforms, etc.).

9) Typical design features used to make sortition workable (because the benefits depend on them)

The claimed advantages usually assume safeguards such as:

  • Adequate pay, job protection, and caregiving support (so non-wealthy citizens can serve).
  • Training, expert testimony, and adversarial briefing (to avoid ignorance being exploited).
  • Strong ethics rules and transparency (asset disclosure, gift bans, anti-lobbying rules).
  • Independent facilitation and procedural rules (to keep deliberation fair).
  • Recall/removal mechanisms for misconduct, and judicial/constitutional constraints to prevent abuses.

These are presented as necessary to preserve fairness and resist elite manipulation even without elections.

Bottom line

Advocates of nationwide sortition argue it could:

  • Increase fairness by giving all citizens a realistic, equal chance to govern and by reducing distortions from money and campaigning.
  • Reduce elite influence by eliminating fundraising, weakening party gatekeeping, and preventing a permanent political class.
  • Enhance democratic representation by producing governing bodies that more closely mirror the population and focus on deliberation rather than electoral strategy.

Let’s not get carried away.

Central to the promise of American democracy is the empowerment of the “common man and woman.” Yet, electoral politics has become the province of elites — wealthy, well-connected, or celebrity candidates who possess the resources and skills to endure costly, bruising campaigns. Today, I stand before you to challenge the very foundation of our political system — not because I disdain democracy, but because I believe we can do better. I call upon us all to reimagine our shared future, to abolish the corrosive charade of elections and instead embrace sortition — the random selection of our representatives from among ordinary citizens.

Now, you may wonder: why would we relinquish our long-prized elections? Because elections, as we know them today, have become breeding grounds for inequality, corruption, and disillusionment. They favor the wealthy, the connected, the charismatic performers over the honest and capable voices of everyday Americans. Campaigns are flooded with special interest money. Lobbyists whisper in elected ears. Career politicians craft carefully scripted personas to secure votes, often at the expense of truth and integrity. The system is rigged — not for the people, but for power itself.

Sortition shatters this broken paradigm. It gives every citizen — regardless of wealth, race, or background — an equal chance to serve their country. No longer will political office be the privilege of millionaires or dynasties. Instead, it will empower teachers, nurses, factory workers, farmers, students, and small business owners — the real heartbeat of America — to lead our nation. It will return government to where it truly belongs: in the hands of the people.

Imagine a Congress that looks like America because it literally is America — diverse in thought, experience, and background. A government where officials owe their duty solely to their nation, not to donors or party bosses. A leadership of citizens beholden not to re-election ambitions but to the solemn responsibility of stewardship, knowing their term is temporary and their duty sacred.

Sortition strips away the corrupting influence of money and media spectacle. It eliminates gerrymandering, vote suppression, and election interference. It makes our democracy fairer, purer, more genuine — by giving everyone the same chance to represent or be represented.

This is not a radical fantasy. Ancient Athens, the birthplace of democracy, used sortition to great effect. Today, citizen juries decide matters of life and death because we trust the fairness of random selection and the common sense of ordinary people. Why shouldn’t we entrust our governance to the same?

Abolishing elections in favor of sortition is not a rejection of democracy — it is its renaissance. It is the fulfillment of the American promise: that this nation shall be governed of the people, by the people, and for the people.

Let us dare to dream bigger. Let us wrest power away from the corrupting grips of money and ambition and return it to the citizenry. Let us build a government that is humble, just, representative, and fair.

The time has come to empower ordinary Americans — all of us — to take our rightful place as the true leaders of this great nation.

Thank you.
